source.title: EHR foundation models improve robustness in the presence of temporal distribution shift
source.authors: Lin Lawrence Guo; E. Steinberg; S. Fleming; J. Posada; J. Lemmon; Stephen R. Pfohl; N. Shah; J. Fries; Lillian Sung

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates how pretraining-set size affects EHR foundation-model performance, extending scale-related findings to structured clinical records and downstream clinical prediction tasks. It does not test language-model loss power laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study varies EHR pretraining data size from 36 K to 1.8 M patients and reports downstream performance and correlations with pretraining performance. Its main-text descriptions do not provide numerical scaling slopes or correlation coefficients; referenced supplementary tables and figures are not included here. The paper cites the original scaling-law work but does not test its parameter-count, compute, or loss-extrapolation claims. Its temporal-robustness comparisons and reclassification results do not themselves test the versions unless they are tied to scale or pretraining performance.
record.test_reason: The study pretrains autoregressive EHR code-sequence models (GRU and transformer) on 36K to 1.8M patients. It reports how frozen-representation downstream clinical performance changes with pretraining-set size, and how pretraining loss correlates with downstream loss. That bears on V6 in a new, non-text setting. No power law is fitted (only linear slopes across about 1.7 orders of magnitude of data), and model size and compute are not varied, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct, but it omits the main conclusion. The authors conclude that CLMBR-LR beat count-LR in discrimination and often decayed less under temporal shift. They add that transformer CLMBR performance and robustness kept improving with more pretraining data, while GRU did better at small sizes. Pretraining loss correlated with downstream loss in some tasks but not all. Overall, pretraining EHR foundation models at scale is useful.
record.recipe_differences: Scales EHR pretraining-set size and assesses downstream clinical prediction performance; it does not fit language-model held-out loss power laws or vary model size or training compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Architecture changes the reported scaling pattern: GRU generally performs better at smaller pretraining sizes, while transformer discrimination scales better at larger sizes. Calibration scaling is heterogeneous.

fits_no_version.finding: The data-scaling slope depends on architecture family: GRU is better at small pretraining sizes, while the transformer scales better and overtakes it at larger sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The benefit from additional pretraining data differs by architecture family (inductive bias), not only by size.

record.problems: The study uses a single clinical dataset and a limited number of outcomes. It examines only pretraining-set size, not model size or compute. Numerical scaling slopes and Pearson coefficients are not given in the supplied main text, and calibration results are described as heterogeneous.
record.rows_left_out: No rows left out. The general comparisons of CLMBR-LR with count-LR and the reclassification analysis were not included because they do not report scale-dependent results or pretraining-to-downstream predictability.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute, and no power-law fit.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count; only GRU versus transformer families are compared.
EHR data is scaled, but no power-law form for loss is tested.
Model-size and compute scaling are not varied. No functional form beyond a linear slope is fitted. The 30-day readmission correlation is not reported in the main text.

missing.what: Per-task and per-metric slopes of performance versus pretraining-set size for each architecture
missing.locator: Supplementary Tables S6 and S7; Figure 5

missing.what: Pearson coefficients for pretraining versus downstream loss, including the 30-day readmission task (implied not to correlate)
Transformer OOD robustness improving with pretraining size (2020–2021 year group)

record.verdict_notes: The setting is EHR code-sequence models, not language models. Scale is pretraining patients only (36K to 1.8M); model size is up to 42M parameters and is not varied. Larger pretraining sets are confounded with temporal closeness to the test years. The upstream-downstream correlation is across hyperparameter configurations, not scale.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute, and power-law form over several orders of magnitude.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Fixed-compute allocation between parameters and tokens, and its trend with compute.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same power-law form holds in other modalities or training regimes; the study scales EHR pretraining data but does not test a power law for loss.
The results concern EHR models and four clinical prediction tasks; they do not establish downstream predictability for general language models or other tasks.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup and fitting choices, and systematic curve bending.

rows.subject: transformer-based CLMBR
rows.stage_stated: EHR self-supervised pretraining; representations used for downstream logistic regression
rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream performance across pretraining-set sizes.
rows.measure: Downstream discrimination performance as pretraining-set size increased
rows.value: Transformer-based CLMBR exhibited better scaling of discrimination performance to pretraining-set size, outperforming GRU-based CLMBR at larger pretraining-set sizes.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this scaling result
rows.note: The statement aggregates results across the plotted tasks and year groups; numerical scores and slopes are referred to in supplementary tables not included in the supplied text.
rows.check: State is acceptable, but the result is confounded: larger pretraining sets also span years closer to the test sets, which the authors say may explain some gains. Only fitted linear slopes are reported (Supp. Table S7, not supplied), so 'predictable' functional form is untested. The text also says transformer OOD robustness improved with size.

rows.operation_detail: Compared downstream performance across pretraining-set sizes.
rows.measure: Downstream discrimination performance as pretraining-set size increased
rows.value: GRU-based CLMBR generally performed better with smaller pretraining-set sizes.
rows.uncertainty: not stated for this scaling result
rows.note: The reported advantage is at smaller data sizes; the text does not give numerical values or task-specific exceptions.
rows.check: The row records a between-architecture ranking (GRU better at small sizes), not whether GRU performance itself rises with pretraining size. The text only implies GRU improved less than the transformer; no GRU slope is given in the main text.

relationships.condition: Transformer-based CLMBR discrimination versus pretraining-set size; pretraining-loss correlation for long LOS and ICU admission
relationships.reason: Transformer discrimination improved as pretraining data grew (R1), though data size is confounded with temporal proximity. Pretraining loss correlated strongly with downstream loss for long LOS and ICU admission (R4).
relationships.display_finding: Discrimination improved with larger pretraining datasets despite confounding by temporal proximity, and pretraining loss strongly correlated with downstream loss for long stays and ICU admission.

relationships.condition: Calibration metric; hospital-mortality correlation; tasks not covered
relationships.reason: Calibration scaling was heterogeneous (R3). The mortality correlation ranged from weak to strong (R5). The authors say the correlation held in 'some tasks, but not all'.
relationships.display_finding: Calibration scaling is heterogeneous, mortality correlations range from weak to strong, and the relationship holds for some tasks but fails for others.
